name: Electric tweezers
lead: Electric tweezers, also sold as tweezer epilators, are handheld devices that combine a pair of tweezers with a high-frequency electrical signal. The user grips a single hair, and pressing a side button closes the tips and switches on the signal, which is meant to weaken the hair's connection to its root and stop regrowth in a way similar to electrolysis.[1] People use them for grooming facial and body hair, such as shaping brows or removing stray hairs on the upper lip and chin, with the aim of a cleaner, smoother look that does not need constant re-plucking.

Each hair is treated individually and needs several seconds of application, so the process is slower than ordinary plucking.[1] The US Food and Drug Administration defines permanent hair removal, and Wikipedia reports that these devices have not been able to meet that definition.[1] Professional electrology, by comparison, inserts a fine probe into each follicle and uses galvanic, thermolysis or blend current to destroy the hair-producing cells.[2]
The term also appears in physics, where electric tweezers use electric fields to manipulate nanoparticles, which is unrelated to grooming.[3] Powered motorised tweezers have also been patented.[4]
infobox: High-frequency signal at tweezer tip to affect hair root
One hair at a time, several seconds each

paras: Ordinary tweezers have been used for plucking hair since antiquity, with metal examples from Mesopotamia and India around 3000 BC.[5] Electric versions put a button on the handle: pressing it closes the tips and sends a high-frequency signal at the same moment.[1] Products are sometimes labelled electrolysis tweezer epilators, though Wikipedia notes they work quite differently from standard epilators.[1]

Because they handle one hair at a time, electric tweezers are used on small, visible areas, for example eyebrow edges, upper lip, chin and stray hairs on the face. The appeal is a smoother look with fewer regrowing hairs, compared with plucking or shaving that needs repeating.[1]

The FDA defines permanent hair removal, and the devices have not been able to meet that definition, according to Wikipedia; the article adds that a device could meet the definition yet still be ineffective for some people.[1] It also reports that the FDA has suggested many users end up using them as ordinary tweezers, a statement the article marks as lacking a citation.[1] In professional electrolysis, results are described as depending on operator skill, hair type, skin condition and the client's pain threshold.[2]
Published work titled "electric tweezers" concerns nanoparticle manipulation, not cosmetic devices.[3] Patent filings from 2006 describe powered or electric tweezer mechanisms.[4]
No studies found of consumer electric tweezers for hair removal. Electrolysis delivered by a trained practitioner is a separate method.[2]

card.summary: Battery-powered pluckers, some sold with a claim of damaging the root; no human studies found.
card.note: Efficacy and safety claims for the electrified type are untested in the sources found.

quick.overview:
Electric tweezers are powered tweezers sold for plucking hair; some are described as sending an electrical signal to the root.

No clinical evidence was found.
quick.mechanism: Motorised grip, or an electrical signal at the tip intended to damage the root.
quick.risks: No safety data were found; skin irritation is a general plucking risk.

chain: High-frequency signal is applied to the hair
Signal is meant to weaken the root
Fewer regrowing hairs in treated spots
angle.text: Users aim to remove stray facial or body hairs and have them return less often than with plain plucking. Each hair is treated one at a time, which suits small areas such as brows, upper lip and chin.
